summary: Explains how to use the Camellia block cipher for encryption in the OpenPGP protocol, giving the identifiers and details needed for implementations. It is informational and was later replaced by RFC 9580, the revised OpenPGP specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5581 defines how OpenPGP identifies and uses the Camellia symmetric cipher. Implementations may support it, but senders need to consider whether recipients can decrypt with it; RFC 9580 later replaced this document.

questions: how to use camellia in pgp
how to use camellia in openpgp
subtitle: The algorithm identifiers and rules for using Camellia in OpenPGP

tldr.problem: OpenPGP can support different symmetric ciphers, and implementations need a defined way to identify Camellia.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns OpenPGP algorithm numbers to Camellia's three key lengths and permits implementations to support it optionally.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5581 updates RFC 4880 and was later obsoleted by RFC 9580.

sections.title: Camellia in OpenPGP
sections.content:
OpenPGP can support different symmetric ciphers. This document gives the information needed to use Camellia, a symmetric block cipher with a 128-bit block size and keys of 128, 192 or 256 bits.

The RFC references the Camellia algorithm description in RFC 3713 and updates the OpenPGP message-format specification, RFC 4880.
sections.plainLanguage: Camellia is one cipher that OpenPGP can use to protect data. This RFC explains how OpenPGP identifies its different key lengths.

sections.title: OpenPGP Algorithm Numbers
sections.content:
OpenPGP identifies a symmetric-key algorithm with a number. This RFC assigns number 11 to Camellia with a 128-bit key, number 12 to a 192-bit key, and number 13 to a 256-bit key.

These identifiers let OpenPGP implementations distinguish the Camellia key length when using the cipher.
sections.plainLanguage: OpenPGP uses a number to identify which Camellia key length a message uses. The three numbers in this RFC each match one of the defined key lengths.

sections.title: Optional Support and Interoperability
sections.content:
OpenPGP applications MAY implement Camellia. If an application implements it, the cipher may be used anywhere a symmetric cipher is usable in OpenPGP and follows the same usage requirements as other symmetric ciphers, including algorithm preferences.

The RFC warns of interoperability problems if an optional cipher encrypts a private key or a symmetrically encrypted message. Those cases do not use the algorithm-preference system to avoid the problem, so the intended recipient needs to support the cipher. At publication, the RFC reports no known weak keys and says implementers should check current cryptographic literature.
sections.plainLanguage: Support for Camellia is optional. Before using it for a private key or a symmetrically encrypted message, make sure the recipient can decrypt it.
